title: Jeremiah on Trial for His Life
summary: Early in Jehoiakim's reign Jeremiah stands in the temple court and warns that if the people will not listen, the LORD will make the temple like Shiloh. Priests, prophets, and people seize him and demand his death, but the royal officials hold a hearing, some elders recall that King Hezekiah spared the prophet Micah for a similar message, and Jeremiah is released. The chapter adds that another prophet, Uriah, was not so fortunate: Jehoiakim had him hunted down in Egypt and killed.
story: Chapter 26 opens the second half of the book, which tells more stories about Jeremiah's life and fewer poems. It is the narrative companion to the temple sermon of chapter 7, which gives the sermon itself; here we learn what it cost him. The chapter sets the pattern for everything that follows: the religious establishment wants Jeremiah dead, some officials protect him, and the king is hostile. It also introduces the family of Shaphan, whose members shelter Jeremiah repeatedly (Ahikam here, and later Gemariah in chapter 36 and Gedaliah in chapters 39 to 41). Placed right after the seventy-years prophecy of chapter 25, it shows why judgment came: the nation put the messenger on trial instead of heeding the message.
historical:
The phrase “at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim” points to about 609 or 608 BC. Josiah, Judah's reforming king, had been killed at Megiddo in 609 BC fighting Pharaoh Neco of Egypt. Neco deposed Josiah's son Jehoahaz after three months and placed another son, Eliakim, on the throne, renaming him Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:29-35). Jehoiakim ruled as an Egyptian vassal and taxed the land heavily to pay tribute, which helps explain why Uriah fled to Egypt and why Jehoiakim could have him extradited from there.

The elders cite Micah of Moresheth, who prophesied under Hezekiah (who reigned roughly 715 to 686 BC), and quote Micah 3:12 almost exactly. This is the only place in the prophetic books where one prophet is cited by name as a precedent. Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood in the days of Eli, had been destroyed long before, probably in the Philistine wars after the ark was captured (1 Samuel 4; Psalm 78:60). The Shaphan named in verse 24 was the royal secretary who read the rediscovered book of the law to Josiah (2 Kings 22:8-14), and his son Ahikam was among those Josiah sent to consult the prophetess Huldah.
cultural:
The scene is a legal proceeding. The accusers are the priests and prophets; the court is made up of the king's officials, who come up from the palace and sit in the gate, the traditional place of judgment in an Israelite town. The elders, respected heads of families and clans, cite precedent, and the people swing from one side to the other. The charge is capital: in Deuteronomy 18:20 a prophet who speaks in the LORD's name what he was not commanded to speak must die. Jeremiah's accusers assume that a word against the temple cannot come from the LORD, because the temple was the LORD's own house.

That assumption had deep roots. Jerusalem had survived the Assyrian siege of 701 BC in Hezekiah's day, and many believed the city was inviolable. To compare the temple with Shiloh was to say that God's presence was not a permanent guarantee. The “burial place of the common people” (verse 23) was a public burial ground, probably in the Kidron valley (compare 2 Kings 23:6), so Uriah was denied an honorable family tomb.
literary: The chapter is a tightly told courtroom drama. God's command (verses 1 to 6) is followed by the arrest (7 to 9), the hearing with accusation and defense (10 to 15), the verdict (16), and the precedent cited by the elders (17 to 19). Two short episodes then balance each other: Uriah, who fled and was killed (20 to 23), and Jeremiah, who was protected by Ahikam (24). The word “relent” (verses 3, 13, and 19) runs through the chapter: God hopes to relent, Jeremiah calls on the people so that God may relent, and the elders remember that he did relent in Hezekiah's day. The story's theme is that a prophet's word of doom is also an invitation.

outline.t: The temple sermon: listen, or this house will be like Shiloh
Seized and accused by priests and prophets
The verdict and the precedent of Micah
The prophet Uriah hunted down and killed
Ahikam son of Shaphan protects Jeremiah

doctrines.note: God sends Jeremiah hoping that the people “will listen and turn” (verse 3) so that he may relent. Many prophecies of judgment are conditional warnings, and the elders' memory of Hezekiah proves that turning to God could change the outcome.

The religious leaders judged Jeremiah by what they already believed about the temple rather than by God's covenant word. The chapter warns that sacred institutions can become the grounds for rejecting the very word that established them.
Uriah's death shows that faithfulness does not guarantee safety. Jeremiah is spared and Uriah is not, though both spoke the same message; the chapter reports both without explaining the difference.

words.note: Nacham, to relent or change one's mind, sometimes translated repent when used of God. It does not mean God made a mistake; it describes his freedom to respond to human repentance by withdrawing a threatened judgment (compare 18:7-10 and Jonah 3:10).

Shiloh, the town north of Jerusalem where the tabernacle stood before the monarchy. Its ruin was a standing reminder that God had once abandoned a place where his name dwelt. Naming it in the temple court was deeply provocative.
Torah, instruction or law. It covers more than legal rules; it is the whole teaching God gave Israel to shape its life. Verse 4 ties listening to God with walking in his torah.

christ: Jeremiah's trial is one of the Old Testament stories that the Gospels' account of Jesus most closely resembles. Jesus also spoke of the temple's destruction (Mark 13:2), was accused of threatening the temple (Mark 14:58), was tried before religious leaders who wanted his death, and was handed to the ruler of the day. Jesus himself quoted Jeremiah's temple sermon when he cleared the temple courts, calling it a den of robbers (Mark 11:17, citing Jeremiah 7:11). He grieved over Jerusalem as the city that kills the prophets (Matthew 23:37), a line that fits Uriah's fate exactly. The difference is decisive: Jeremiah was spared, but Jesus was not, and the innocent blood Jeremiah warned about was shed in Jesus' death. Stephen, the first Christian martyr, was later accused in almost the same terms of speaking against the holy place (Acts 6:13-14).

hard.q: If God declared disaster and then relented, does he change his mind? Were his warnings real?
hard.a: The chapter treats God's threats as real and his relenting as real. Many of the Bible's prophecies of judgment are conditional, even when the condition isn't spoken, as Jeremiah 18:7-10 explains: if a nation turns from evil, God will relent of the disaster he planned. Jonah's preaching to Nineveh works the same way. Theologians have explained this differently. Some stress that God's purpose is unchanging and that his relenting was always part of that purpose, which included the people's response. Others stress that the Bible presents God as genuinely responsive to prayer and repentance in time. Both agree that the warnings were meant to be heeded and that the elders drew the right lesson from Micah's case: a word of judgment is also a call to turn.

questions: The priests and prophets could not imagine that God would allow his own temple to be destroyed. What religious certainties might keep people today from hearing a hard word?
Ahikam risked his standing to protect Jeremiah. Who in your life has stood beside you when it cost them something, and whom could you stand beside?
Uriah died and Jeremiah lived. How do you hold onto faith when faithfulness does not end well in this life?
